section.title: What is RTPProxy
section.para: The RTPProxy is a high-performance software proxy for RTP streams that can work together with Sippy B2BUA, Kamailio, OpenSIPS and SER (SIP Express Router).

note.para: The latest stable version is RTPProxy 3.2

section.title: Backstory
section.para: RTPProxy was originally developed by Maxim Sobolyev in 2003 with a purpose of VoIP calls facilitation to/from SIP User Agents located behind NAT or firewalls. That time, there were a few cases where direct end-to-end communication between users behind the NAT was not possible. RTPProxy, in common with a SIP proxy, overcomes those obstacles by acting as an intermediary point for the RTP streams.
Afterwards, the RTPProxy has become widely used by VoIP service providers that are in a demand for optimizing a traffic flow in their networks.

Later on it became apparent that there are many other possible uses of this software. It can be used in common with a signaling element (SIP Proxy or SIP B2BUA) to build complex VoIP networks, to optimize a traffic flow, to collect voice quality information and so on.
RTPProxy is now actively developed and maintained by the Sippy Software, Inc. and is available on GitHub of Sippy Labs - https://github.com/sippy/rtpproxy.

Over the years, many other individuals and organizations have contributed features and fixes into the code base, including Vonage, SipPulse, Voicenter, RateTel, either directly or by sponsoring respective development efforts (often both).

section.title: Capabilities
section.para: Originally it was designed for handling of NAT scenarios. It can also act as a generic media relay, as well as a gateway for RTP sessions between IPv4 and IPv6 networks.
It can perform a number of additional functions on RTP streams, including call recording, playing pre-recorded announcements, real-time stream copying and RTP payload re-framing.

The RTPProxy supports some advanced features, such as remote control mode, allowing a building of scalable distributed SIP VoIP networks. The rtpproxy modules of OpenSIPS and Kamailio (both descendants of the SIP Express Router, whose nathelper module originally provided this functionality), as well as the Sippy B2BUA, allow using multiple RTPProxy instances running on remote machines for fault-tolerance and load-balancing purposes.
An advanced high-capacity clustering and a load balancing is available through the use of RTP Cluster middleware.
The software also supports MOH/pre-recorded prompts injection, video relaying and RTP session recording to a local file or remote UDP listener(s).

listitem.para: Firstly, when a SIP proxy receives an INVITE request, it extracts a call-id from it and hands it to the proxy via the control socket. Then, in its turn, a proxy looks for an existing session with the same id. If the session exists, it returns a UDP port for that session. In case it doesn't exist, it creates a new session and binds it to a free UDP port, randomly selected from the range specified at the start time, and returns the number of that port to a SIP proxy called it. Upon receiving a reply from the proxy, SIP Proxy (Sippy B2BUA, OpenSIPS or Kamailio) in its turn replaces media IP:port in the SDP body, in order to point to the media proxy and then it forwards a request as usually.

When it comes to receiving of non-negative SIP reply with the SDP body, then SIP proxy again extracts call-id from it and hands it to the rtpproxy. In this case the rtpproxy does not allocate a new session, if it doesn't exist. But simply performs a lookup among existing sessions and returns either a port number if the session is found, or an error code indicating that there is no session with such id. Upon receiving a positive reply from the rtpproxy, SIP Proxy (Sippy B2BUA, OpenSIPS or Kamailio) replaces media IP:port in the SDP body of that SIP reply, in order to point to the rtpproxy and then forwards this reply as usually.

After the session has been created, the rtpproxy listens on the ports it has allocated for that session and relays UDP packets between the call parties. Initially, packets are sent to the addresses provided by the SIP proxy, i.e. taken from the SDP. Once a packet is received from a party, the proxy "latches" to the source ip:port of that packet and uses it as the address of that party from then on, which allows reaching parties located behind NAT. Latching is not done for parties set up as asymmetric.

important.para: A good advantage of the RTPProxy is, that it tracks idle time for each existing session (the period of time within which no packets were relayed) and automatically cleans up a session, idle time of which exceeds the value specified at the command line (60 seconds by default).

section.title: Content of the Package
section.para: The RTPProxy package by default provides the following components:

listitem.para: rtpproxy - main RTP proxy server binary (production build)
rtpproxy_debug - Main RTP proxy server binary (debug and profiling build)
makeann - Utility to pre-encode prompts and announcements (production build)
makeann_debug - Utility to pre-encode prompts and announcements (debug and profiling build, built but not installed)
extractaudio - Utility to convert recorded sessions into plain audio files (production build, only built if libsndfile is available)
extractaudio_debug - Utility to convert recorded sessions into plain audio files (debug and profiling build, built but not installed)

section.title: Pre-built RTPProxy
section.para: In case you want to use a pre-built RTPProxy package, then use your system's package manager to set this up:
dpkg - for Debian based systems (including Ubuntu), when installing .deb packages.
apt-get / aptitude - for Debian based systems (including Ubuntu), when installing from a repository.
rpm - for RPM based systems, when installing .rpm packages.
pkg - for FreeBSD when installing from a repository or packages.
Starting with version 3.2.0, packages for several Debian and Ubuntu releases are attached to each release on the GitHub releases page.
Official Docker images are published to Docker Hub (sippylabs/rtpproxy) and GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/sippy/rtpproxy) with every release and every commit to the master branch.
In case you want to compile RTPProxy from sources, use the following section "Compilation from sources".

simplesect.title: Installing Dependencies
simplesect.para: The RTPProxy package has several optional dependencies that are detected at the configure stage and an appropriate functionality is enabled.
Those dependencies and their impact on the RTPProxy build are listed below:

listitem.para: bcg729 - Enables G.729 support in several tools.
libsndfile - Required to build extractaudio, which uses it to save decoded audio in a number of popular audio formats.
libg722 - Enables G.722 support in several tools.
libsrtp2 (preferred) or libsrtp - Enables decoding recordings of SRTP streams. Together with OpenSSL, also enables building the dtls_gw and ice_lite modules.
libgsm - Enables GSM 06.10 support in several tools.

libsystemd-dev - allows for a tighter systemd integration.
Also requires --enable-systemd configure argument to enable. See section on enabling systemd support for details.

libelperiodic - Required by several internal tools that are used by an automated testing framework. If it is not installed on the system, the copy bundled as a git submodule is built and used instead.
tcpdump - Test framework requires it to capture traffic and verify PCAP decoding features. make check will fail if it's not installed.
sudo - Test framework requires it to run the tcpdump at elevated privileges. make check will fail if it's not installed.

important.para: Do not forget about your compiler! To build this version of the RTPProxy you would need either:

listitem.para: GCC compiler, version 11 or higher, or
Clang compiler, version 11 or higher

important.para: Those are the oldest versions tested by the continuous integration.

simplesect.para: Clone the source code (into a directory where you want to store compilation sources, usually it's /usr/src/). The master branch contains the latest development version, use a release tag (e.g. v3.2.0) instead to build a stable release:

simplesect.para: After a successful compilation, you have the following binaries

After the compilation is done, you have a binary file stored in the /usr/local/bin/ folder. You can test this out, checking the version of the rtpproxy: /usr/local/bin/rtpproxy -V
Main RTP proxy server binary - debug and profiling build.
You will also have a second binary file for debug and profiling: /usr/local/bin/rtpproxy_debug

chapter.title: Getting Started

highlights.para: A good way to maintain your RTPProxy is to start it using a certain Service Manager, such as systemd.
systemd is the default service manager on most Linux distributions:

listitem.para: Ubuntu 15.04 is the first version (of Ubuntu) that uses systemd by default;
Debian 8 (Jessie) is the first version (of Debian) that uses systemd by default;
There is a huge list of other distributions, that use the systemd as a System Manager by default now as well (OpenSUSE, Mint, Mageia etc.) .

chapter.para: In case you have a system, that doesn't support the systemd, you can use any other Service Managers as you want to (e.g. init.d start scripts in Debian systems older than 8th one).
That said, systemd is the recommended solution, because it provides the following capabilities:

listitem.para: Define a list of options in a separate environment file, and use those options as a variable in the start row 'ExecStart='
You're able to react on a failure of an application using a special parameter 'OnFailure=' (and to send notification for e.g.)
You can specify a list of pre-actions to be performed, before systemd launches binary file 'ExecStartPre=' (e.g. creation of /var/run/rtpproxy directory and adding user/group rights to it)
As well as you can add pre-start actions, you can perform post-stop actions for cases when application stops running 'ExecStopPost=' (e.g. deletion of the /var/run/rtpproxy directory)
You can set a policy for cases when application stops improperly (not a manual stop of the application), e.g. restarting always with 'Restart=always'
You may also want to add a time delay between restart attempts with 'RestartSec=5'

You can deal with different things related to logging or syslogging (e.g. changing of a name identifier when writing to a syslog 'SyslogIdentifier=' or specifying a different logfacility level with 'StandardOutput=' and 'StandardError=' )
User/Group to be used for running an application
and many many other things..

chapter.para: The link to an instance of the systemd service file (for the RTPProxy): systemd configuration file instance -> Instance of the systemd service file
After you downloaded your systemd service file, adjust OPTIONS parameters.
Set your own IP address for listening, or leave it with 0.0.0.0 (manual way)

Set upper bound on number of file descriptors the rtpproxy service instance might be using. Rule of thumb is that 4 file descriptors are needed for a fully established session (two RTP endpoints and two RTCP ones).

important.para: Make the value reasonably high to match your load expectations in terms of number of concurrent sessions but not excessively high, as it may cause rtpproxy to fail initialization because operating system usually also enforces upper bound on this value that varies from system to system:

chapter.para: You may also want to change a port range for opening UDP ports:
Change your log facility level if you want to:
Another great reason to use systemd, is a possibility of systemd to create control sockets for rtpproxy.

The benefit of this is that the control socket stays in place while rtpproxy is down for some reason, e.g. being restarted. Clients (such as OpenSIPS or Kamailio) connecting to it during that time are not refused: their connections are queued and get served once rtpproxy is back (they can still get timeout errors if that takes too long). Connections that were already open when rtpproxy went down are lost.
To let this be working, follow this guide: Configuration section -> 5. Configuration of control socket.
Other than that, for better view of how to configure your startup line, you can use this Configuration section.
After you're done with customizing of your systemd service file for RTPProxy, follow this sequence to finish it:

listitem.para: copy it to the /etc/systemd/system/ directory
reload systemd configuration with: bash> sudo systemctl daemon-reload
enable the service: bash> sudo systemctl enable rtpproxy.service

chapter.title: Configuration
chapter.para: Historically, primary configuration method for the RTPProxy was done via command-line parameters. Starting with version 2.2 certain advanced parameters (particularly loadable modules configuration) have been moved into configuration file.

simplesect.title: OPTIONS
simplesect.para: The following command-line parameters are supported:

section.title: Configuration File
section.para: Configuration of the loadable modules is read from a configuration file in the UCL format, specified with the --config command-line option. See Modules for the available modules and their parameters. An example is provided in doc/rtpproxy.conf.sample.

section.title: Startup Script
section.para: The way you integrate RTPProxy into your system startup sequence is highly OS-version dependent. If you are using a pre-built RTPProxy package then most likely such method will be provided as part of that package and the best course of actions is to use that facility.

However, if you are a package maintainer or system builder you might need to create such configuration from scratch. In the next sections we would provide some basic guidelines on how to launch RTPProxy in some common cases.

simplesect.title: Systemd based systems
simplesect.para: On most modern Linux-based systems systemd is the recommended method to start the RTPProxy.
simplesect.programlisting:
[Unit] Description=RTPProxy media server After=network.target Requires=network.target
[Service] Type=simple PIDFile=/var/run/rtpproxy/rtpproxy.pid Environment='OPTIONS= -f -L 4096 -l 0.0.0.0 -m 10000 -M 20000 -d INFO:LOG_LOCAL5'
Restart=always RestartSec=5
ExecStartPre=-/bin/mkdir /var/run/rtpproxy ExecStartPre=-/bin/chown rtpproxy:rtpproxy /var/run/rtpproxy
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/rtpproxy -p /var/run/rtpproxy/rtpproxy.pid -s unix:/var/run/rtpproxy/rtpproxy.sock \ -u rtpproxy:rtpproxy -n unix:/var/run/rtpproxy/rtpproxy_timeout.sock $OPTIONS ExecStop=/usr/bin/pkill -F /var/run/rtpproxy/rtpproxy.pid
ExecStopPost=-/bin/rm -R /var/run/rtpproxy
SyslogIdentifier=rtpproxy SyslogFacility=local5
TimeoutStartSec=10 TimeoutStopSec=10
[Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target
simplesect.para: The source tree also contains the unit files used for packaging, rpm/rtpproxy.service and rpm/rtpproxy.socket, which are installed by the Debian packages. They use systemd socket activation, which requires building with --enable-systemd, see below.

section.title: Logging
section.para: Logging is a very important aspect of the RTPProxy operation that should not be overlooked. In our experience, properly configured and tested RTPProxy instance can keep running unattended literally for many years non-stop. Yet, various issues with a particular session and/or endpoint would inevitably pop-up over time, so it's of utter importance to setup logging and log management in a manner that is durable and forward-looking. Allowing someone to perform a post-mortem investigation of particular issue that happened days, if not weeks, ago with a relative ease.
Some of the considerations one should have in mind while configuring logging is:

listitem.para: How much storage my system has for the RTPProxy to use?
What is the typical amount of time it takes for my user to report an issue and get it escalated to the DevOps team?
What is the typical amount of time it takes for the DevOps team to act on issue and look at the logs in question?
How much detail do I need? The answer to this might depend on whether this is a development/QA or a production system.
Are there any other non-technical considerations that might influence those decisions? For example: data protection laws, law enforcement requirements etc.
First of all you need to create a file you will use for logging and give it proper permissions (according to a user/group starting RTPProxy):
Then define a log facility for it in rsyslog configuration file (add a row at the bottom of the file) and restart rsyslog server:
next step add a log rotation configuration for this log file (that's a good way of handling overfilled log files):
listitem.programlisting: /var/log/rtpproxy.log { missingok compress delaycompress notifempty copytruncate rotate 5 daily }

listitem.para: Now add a log facility level to your start row of the RTPProxy:
Reload systemd configuration (to apply previous change) and restart your RTPProxy server. Now logging should be done using new output file:

section.title: Configuration of control socket (using systemd)
section.para: As it was said earlier, keeping of the control socket using systemd, is a good reason to start using systemd.
A configuration process is pretty simple, there are just a few steps you need to implement to start using of it.
1. Firstly, you need to install package requirements: libsystemd-dev
2. Secondly, you need to compile rtpproxy with a systemd flag (a usual compilation process, just add an option to a configure execution): ./configure --enable-systemd
3. A third step, you need to create rtpproxy.socket systemd unit file, that will be responsible for keeping your control socket:
An example:
/etc/systemd/system/rtpproxy.socket (enabling it with systemctl enable creates the link in sockets.target.wants)

para.programlisting:
[Socket] ListenStream=/var/run/rtpproxy/rtpproxy.sock SocketUser=rtpproxy SocketGroup=rtpproxy SocketMode=0660 ExecStartPost=-/bin/chown rtpproxy:rtpproxy /var/run/rtpproxy
[Install] WantedBy=sockets.target

section.para: The SIP proxy has to be able to write to the socket, so make sure it runs as a member of the rtpproxy group.
4. Set a parameter in startup row of rtpproxy.service unit (you don't need to provide a path to socket file):
an example:
When you're done with all above, do not forget to reload systemd configuration and enable socket unit:
section.programlisting:
bash> sudo systemctl daemon-reload
bash> sudo systemctl enable rtpproxy.socket
section.para: (btw here is a nice article of how to configure systemd socket unit files - http://0pointer.de/blog/projects/socket-activation.html)
Now start rtpproxy.socket and rtpproxy.service just after that:

bash> sudo systemctl start rtpproxy.socket
bash> sudo systemctl start rtpproxy.serviceAt this stage, your rtpproxy.service should catch up a socket created by systemd and start working properly. If you see some kind of errors, then you're missing one of the steps defined above.

chapter.title: Modules
chapter.para: Some of the RTPProxy functionality is implemented as loadable modules. A module can be loaded either via the configuration file, which also allows setting its parameters, or via the --dso command-line option, which only works for modules that take no parameters.

section.title: Loading Modules
section.para: Each module is configured in its own block of the modules section of the configuration file. The name of the block is the name of the module. Unless the load parameter specifies the path to the module's shared object, the module is loaded from libdir/rtpproxy/rtpp_name.so (rtpp_name_debug.so for the debug build). Modules that take no parameters can have an empty block:
The same module can be loaded more than once, each loaded copy being a separate instance, numbered from 1 in the order of loading.

section.title: Controlling Modules
section.para: Modules that are controlled on a per-session basis accept sub-commands appended to the U or L command after &&, in the form Mmodule_id:instance arguments. The module IDs are listed below, and instance is 1 unless the module is loaded more than once. For example, the following command sends S to the first instance of the dtls_gw module:

Several sub-commands can be chained in the same command, each with its own &&. The output of each of them follows the reply to the main command, separated by && too. A failed sub-command is reported as a negative number, while one with no output is reported as 0, or omitted when no sub-command after it has any output.

row.entry: Per-session accounting into a CSV file
Reporting RTCP to a HEP (Homer) collector
Notifying the call controller of DTMF events
Gateway between plain RTP and DTLS-SRTP

section.title: acct_csv
section.para: Writes one record with the session's statistics into a CSV file for each session, when the session ends. A header line with the column names is written when the file is created. The columns include the Call-ID, the from-tag, the session setup and teardown times, and the packet, loss, jitter and SSRC statistics for each direction. The file is re-opened if it is moved or removed, e.g. by log rotation.
The module takes no sub-commands. The parameters are:

listitem.para: Path of the CSV file. A relative path is relative to the directory the rtpproxy was started from. Default: rtpproxy_acct.csv.

section.para: Since the parameter is optional, the module can also be loaded with the --dso command-line option.

section.title: acct_rtcp_hep
section.para: Reports every RTCP packet received, converted to JSON, to a HEP (Homer) collector, using HEPv3.
The module takes no sub-commands. The parameters are:

listitem.para: Address of the collector. Default: 10.0.0.1.
Port of the collector. Default: 9060.
Transport, udp or tcp. Default: udp.
Capture agent ID, from 0 to 4294967295. Default: 101.

section.title: catch_dtmf
section.para: Detects RFC 2833 (RFC 4733) telephone events in the stream and notifies the call controller of each DTMF digit received. Developed in collaboration with the OpenSIPS project. The module takes no parameters.
Detection is enabled per stream with the sub-command:

listitem.para: URL-encoded string that is sent back with each notification.
RTP payload type of the telephone events. Default: 101.
Drop the telephone event packets instead of relaying them.

section.para: Notifications are sent the same way as the session timeout notifications, so notifications have to be enabled for the session: the U/L command has to specify the notification socket (permitted with the -n command-line option) and the notification tag. For each digit, when its last packet is received, the following line is sent:
section.programlisting: U call-id 192.0.2.1 12345 from-tag tcp:192.0.2.100:2222 ntag && M3:1 caller%20dtmf 101
section.para: would result in notifications like:

section.title: dtls_gw
section.para: Gateways between plain RTP (RTP/AVP) and DTLS-SRTP (UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVP) streams, taking care of certificate validation, key negotiation and SRTP encryption/decryption. It can also re-encrypt already encrypted streams back to back, e.g. for recording. Requires the RTPProxy to be built with libsrtp2 (or libsrtp) and OpenSSL. A self-signed certificate is generated when the module starts. The module takes no parameters.
The sub-commands are:

listitem.para: Allocate a DTLS endpoint on the side facing the encrypted party if needed, and return the session mode and the certificate fingerprint to be put into the SDP.
Set up the DTLS endpoint for the remote end in the active or actpass mode, using the fingerprint from its SDP. SSRC verification is enabled if ssrc is given.
The same, for the remote end in the passive mode.
Destroy the DTLS context created by A or P.
Destroy the DTLS context created by S.

section.para: For example, an incoming INVITE with plain RTP answered with DTLS-SRTP by a passive party:
section.programlisting:
U call-id 192.0.2.1 12345 from-tag && M4:1 S 35000 && actpass SHA-256 4A:AD:B9:...
L call-id 192.0.2.2 23456 from-tag to-tag && M4:1 P SHA-256 2C:7F:01:... 35002
section.para: See modules/dtls_gw/README.md for more scenarios.

section.title: ice_lite
section.para: Implements the lite variant of ICE (RFC 5245), allowing ICE-enabled user agents to establish media sessions through the RTPProxy, and RTCP multiplexing and de-multiplexing. Together with dtls_gw, it allows the RTPProxy to act as a WebRTC endpoint. Requires the same libraries as dtls_gw. The module takes no parameters.
The sub-commands are:

listitem.para: Allocate an ICE endpoint if needed, and return the local ice-ufrag, ice-pwd and the ICE candidates (URL-encoded) to offer to the user agent.
Process an ICE offer received from the user agent, allocating an ICE endpoint if needed.
Add a single ICE candidate received from the user agent, as in the a=candidate SDP attribute. Repeat for each candidate.
Destroy the ICE context in the forward direction.
Destroy the ICE context in the reverse direction.

section.para: For example, an incoming INVITE with an ICE offer:
section.programlisting: U call-id 192.0.2.1 12345 from-tag && M5:1 A ufrag pwd && M5:1 C 1 1 UDP 2130706431 192.0.2.1 12345 typ host
section.para: See modules/ice_lite/README.md for more scenarios.

chapter.title: Development
chapter.para: This chapter is intended for developers who embed the RTPProxy into their own applications, or who work on the RTPProxy itself and need to test their changes.

section.title: Embedding RTPProxy: librtpproxy
section.para: The whole RTPProxy engine is also available as a library, librtpproxy, which allows running it inside another process, e.g. a test harness, a fuzzer or an application that needs a media relay of its own without managing a separate daemon.

section.title: Building and Installing
section.para: The library is always built, as it is used by the rtpproxy itself, but it is only installed when the --enable-librtpproxy option is given to the configure script:

This installs a static librtpproxy.a, which already includes the bundled libraries and the modules, and the headers: librtpproxy.h with the main interface and librtpproxy/packetport.h, librtpproxy/packet_ext.h with the packet port interface described below. On Debian and Ubuntu the same files are provided by the rtpproxy-dev package.

Since the library is static, an application has to link with the libraries that the rtpproxy itself has been configured with as well, such as -lsiplog, -lelperiodic, codec and SRTP libraries, -lssl -lcrypto, -lm and -lpthread. If the RTPProxy has been built with LTO, the application has to be linked using the same compiler.

section.title: Interface
section.para: The main interface consists of two functions:

rtpp_main() takes the same arguments as the rtpproxy command line (see Configuration), with argv[0] being the program name, initializes the engine and starts its threads, then returns right away with a handle to the running instance. The library never daemonizes, does not write a PID file, does not change the current directory and does not install any signal handlers, so the -f option is not needed. Instead of exiting the process, an error in the arguments or during initialization makes rtpp_main() return NULL. The global state of the getopt() is saved and restored, so the application is free to use it as well.
rtpp_shutdown() stops the instance, destroys all of its sessions and releases all resources associated with it.

section.title: Controlling an Embedded Instance
section.para: An embedded instance is controlled using the same protocol as a standalone one, via any of the control sockets described in Configuration. The most convenient one is usually the fd:N socket, which makes the instance use a socket created by the application: one end of a connected socket pair becomes a private control channel, with no need to pick an address or a path. Over such a channel commands are written one per line and the replies are read back the same way, without the cookies used by the network control sockets:
The fuzzing harnesses in scripts/fuzz are another example of using the library.

section.title: Packet Ports
section.para: Besides sending and receiving packets via sockets, an embedded instance can exchange them with the application directly, through shared memory packet rings called packet ports. A port is created with rtpp_packetport_ctor(), which takes the capacity of the rings and the policy of flushing the outbound ring (explicitly with rtpp_packetport_flush() or on a timer). The application pushes packets into the instance with rtpp_packetport_push() and friends, and pops the packets sent by the instance with rtpp_packetport_try_pop() and friends.

A port is referenced in the commands by its address, in the RTQ:0xpointer format: as the remote address of a stream, followed by a port tag in place of the port number, to have the instance send the packets of that stream into the port, or as a local address (l modifier) to have the stream receive packets from the port instead of a socket. Packet ports are only available in the library. This interface is a work in progress and may change in the future releases, see src/librtpproxy/packetport.h for the details.

section.title: Testing
section.para: The RTPProxy comes with an extensive suite of integration tests, located in the tests directory. Each test starts one or more rtpproxy instances, drives them via their control sockets, generates and captures media, and compares the results with the reference ones. The tests are also run by the CI on every change, across several operating systems, compilers and architectures.

section.title: Running Tests
section.para: All tests are run with:
A subset of the tests can be selected with the TESTS variable, and several tests can be run in parallel, since none of them depends on pre-determined ports:
section.programlisting: cd tests make -j4 check TESTS="forwarding/forwarding1 playback/playback1"
section.para: A test can also be run directly as sh tests/group/test, which prints the result of each of its steps. Besides the build dependencies of the RTPProxy, the tests need Python 3 with the sippy and parsimonious modules (see python/tools/requirements.txt), ffmpeg and tcpdump. When the tests are run as root, the rtpproxy and the tools are run as the rtpproxy user, via setpriv.

section.title: Writing Tests with RPTL
section.para: New tests are best written using the RTPProxy Testing Language (RPTL), a small scripting language interpreted by python/RPTL/rptl_run.py. An RPTL script starts the rtpproxy instances it needs, sends them commands, checks the replies and runs external tools, passing the ports allocated by one step on to the next ones, so that the tests need neither pre-determined ports nor root privileges and can safely run in parallel.

A script is a sequence of statements, one per line. A socket statement defines a control connection, which with an address of stdio: (or udp:, tcp:, unix: and so on, with nothing after the type) starts a managed rtpproxy instance with the given command line arguments. Every other statement either sends a command to the named socket or runs a built-in, such as .eval:, .sleep:, .include:, .foreach: or .exec:, and can capture the result into a variable, which is then referenced as %%NAME%%, or pass it to a checking function. Any failed check stops the script with an error:
section.programlisting:
# Expects RTPPROXY_BIN to be defined .eval: 0 -> RES_OK .eval: E50 -> SESS_NOTFOUND socket r: stdio: -d info -p /dev/null -> example.rout
r: U call1 127.0.0.1 12000 ftag1 -> validate_port(PORT_O) r: L call1 127.0.0.1 12002 ftag1 ttag1 -> validate_port(PORT_A) .echo: allocated ports %%PORT_O%% and %%PORT_A%% r: D call1 ftag1 -> str_compare(RES_OK) r: D call1 ftag1 -> str_compare(SESS_NOTFOUND)
.close: r
section.para: A test itself is a Bourne shell script, which sets up the environment using the common functions from tests/functions, runs the RPTL script with the RPTL_INT interpreter, passing it the parameters with -D, and then examines the results, e.g. compares the replies logged by the instances with the reference output, or decodes the recorded media with extractaudio and checks its checksum:
section.programlisting:
#!/bin/sh
BASEDIR="`dirname "${0}"`/.." . "${BASEDIR}/functions"
${RPTL_INT} -s "${BASEDIR}/example/example.rptl" \ -D RTPPROXY_BIN="${RTPPROXY}" report "running example.rptl"
${DIFF} "${BASEDIR}/example/example.output" example.rout report "checking rtpproxy replies"
section.para: When the replies contain dynamically allocated ports, the reference output can be a template that matches any port (see scripts/revtempl.py), or the ports can be replaced with a placeholder before the comparison. The test, together with the files it uses, goes into a directory of its group, and is registered in the Makefile.ami of that group, after which the tests/Makefile.in has to be regenerated with automake.

The complete description of the language is available in python/RPTL/README.md, and the tests in tests/recording, tests/session_timeouts, tests/forwarding and tests/playback are written in RPTL and can be used as examples of more complex scenarios, such as running several instances at once, replaying traffic or capturing streams with external tools.
